label: Acts 23:1
text: Paul, looking steadfastly at the council, said, “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.”

label: Acts 23:2
text: The high priest, Ananias, commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth.

label: Acts 23:3
text: Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?”

label: Acts 23:4
text: Those who stood by said, “Do you malign God’s high priest?”

label: Acts 23:5
text: Paul said, “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

label: Acts 23:6
text: But when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!”

label: Acts 23:7
text: When he had said this, an argument arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the crowd was divided.

label: Acts 23:8
text: For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these.

label: Acts 23:9
text: A great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ part stood up, and contended, saying, “We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let’s not fight against God!”

variants.reading: the closing phrase 'let us not fight against God' (KJV) is absent
variants.note: The fetched Wikipedia 'List of omitted Bible verses' (Acts 23:9 (b)): the phrase, which also appears in Acts 5:39, 'does not appear in the earliest and best resources - Papyrus 74, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (original hand), Codex Laudianus' - it first appears in 9th-century codices. The WEB prints it.

label: Acts 23:10
text: When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing that Paul would be torn in pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him by force from among them, and bring him into the barracks.

label: Acts 23:11
text:
The following night, the Lord stood by him, and said,
“Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.”

label: Acts 23:12
text: When it was day, some of the Jews banded together, and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

label: Acts 23:13
text: There were more than forty people who had made this conspiracy.

label: Acts 23:14
text: They came to the chief priests and the elders, and said, “We have bound ourselves under a great curse, to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

label: Acts 23:15
text: Now therefore, you with the council inform the commanding officer that he should bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you were going to judge his case more exactly. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.”

label: Acts 23:16
text: But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.

label: Acts 23:17
text: Paul summoned one of the centurions, and said, “Bring this young man to the commanding officer, for he has something to tell him.”

label: Acts 23:18
text: So he took him, and brought him to the commanding officer, and said, “Paul, the prisoner, summoned me and asked me to bring this young man to you, who has something to tell you.”

label: Acts 23:19
text: The commanding officer took him by the hand, and going aside, asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?”

label: Acts 23:20
text: He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though intending to inquire somewhat more accurately concerning him.

label: Acts 23:21
text: Therefore don’t yield to them, for more than forty men lie in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him. Now they are ready, looking for the promise from you.”

label: Acts 23:22
text: So the commanding officer let the young man go, charging him, “Tell no one that you have revealed these things to me.”

label: Acts 23:23
text: He called to himself two of the centurions, and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen, and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.”

label: Acts 23:24
text: He asked them to provide animals, that they might set Paul on one, and bring him safely to Felix the governor.

label: Acts 23:25
text: He wrote a letter like this:

label: Acts 23:26
text: “Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.

label: Acts 23:27
text: “This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by them, when I came with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.

label: Acts 23:28
text: Desiring to know the cause why they accused him, I brought him down to their council.

label: Acts 23:29
text: I found him to be accused about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment.

label: Acts 23:30
text: When I was told that the Jews lay in wait for the man, I sent him to you immediately, charging his accusers also to bring their accusations against him before you. Farewell.”

label: Acts 23:31
text: So the soldiers, carrying out their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.

label: Acts 23:32
text: But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks.

label: Acts 23:33
text: When they came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.

label: Acts 23:34
text: When the governor had read it, he asked what province he was from. When he understood that he was from Cilicia, he said,

label: Acts 23:35
text: “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.

label: Great-circle distances Jerusalem-Antipatris and Antipatris-Caesarea
method: Haversine distances computed from coordinates: Jerusalem (Temple Mount, 31.778 N, 35.2354 E) to Antipatris (32.105 N, 34.9304 E) = about 46.4 km; Antipatris to Caesarea Maritima (32.5 N, 34.8917 E) = about 44.1 km - a feasible night march of roughly seven hours for infantry plus a next-day cavalry ride, with the road (not the straight line) somewhat longer.

label: Claudius Lysias (the tribune of the cohort in Jerusalem)
note: Named only in the letter of Acts 23:26; the nomen Claudius fits a man enfranchised under Claudius, when new citizens were expected to adopt the emperor's name (Cassius Dio 60.17.7). No source outside Acts names him.

label: Ananias son of Nedebaeus (high priest c. 47-59 CE)
note: Appointed high priest by Herod king of Chalcis (Josephus, Ant. 20.103); sent in bonds to Rome to answer Quadratus (Ant. 20.129-130); under Albinus a 'great hoarder up of money' whose servants took the priests' tithes by violence (Ant. 20.205-206). Whiston's note identifies him as the high priest before whom Paul pleaded.

label: Antonius Felix (procurator of Judea, c. 52-59 CE)
note: Brother of the freedman Pallas; Claudius 'sent Felix, the brother of Pallas, to take care of the affairs of Judea' (Josephus, Ant. 20.137); Tacitus, Hist. 5.9: he 'exercised the power of a king in the spirit of a slave'; Annals 12.54: he thought 'he could do any evil act with impunity'; recalled and nearly punished, saved by his brother Pallas (Ant. 20.182-184).

label: Antipatris
note: City built by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater, lying between Caesarea Maritima and Lydda on the great Roman road from Caesarea to Jerusalem (fetched Wikipedia); Josephus says it was built on the older town Chabarzaba (Kefar Saba).

label: Herod's promontory palace at Caesarea Maritima
note: Herod built his palace on a promontory jutting out into the sea, with a decorative pool surrounded by stoas (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima'); the excavated promontory palace is the standard identification of the 'Herod's palace' (praetorium) where the governors resided.

label: Ananias son of Nedebaeus held the office of high priest
statement: Ananias son of Nedebaeus held the office of high priest (appointed c. 47/48 CE).
note: Office claim: claim:ac-23-02-ananias-office (the titles/offices split) and claim:ac-24-01-ananias-high-priest (Acts 24:1) merged into this oldest id, so Acts 23:2, 23:4 and 24:1 assert it. Josephus, Ant. 20.103: Herod king of Chalcis 'made Ananias, the son of Nebedeu' high priest in place of Joseph son of Camydus, in the period of Cumanus (grade A for the office). The mouth-strike event is claim:ac-23-02-ananias-strikes-paul.

label: The high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by to strike Paul on the mouth
statement: The high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by to strike Paul on the mouth.
note: Event claim split from the merged office claim claim:ac-23-02-ananias-high-priest per the architect's titles/offices ruling; the command to strike is the narrative's own report (Josephus attests the office-holder and tenure, not the blow).

label: The high priest ordered Paul struck on the mouth; Paul protested, 'God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!'
statement: Paul said he had lived in all good conscience; the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth; Paul cried, 'God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?'
note: The event is the narrative's own report. Josephus, Ant. 20.205-206, shows the same Ananias was 'a great hoarder up of money' whose wicked servants took the priests' tithes by violence and beat those who resisted (grade C for the man's recorded violence - a later occasion, under Albinus, not this hearing).

label: Paul quoted the law: 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people'
statement: Apologizing for not knowing Ananias was high priest, Paul quoted the law: 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'
note: The quotation is from Exodus 22:28 (biblical cross-reference, linked related_to). Its use in this dispute is the narrative's own report.

label: Paul declared himself a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees, on trial for the hope and resurrection of the dead
statement: Paul cried out in the council: 'Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!'
note: Paul's Pharisaic self-identification is his own report (22:3; Phil 3:5 is a biblical cross-reference); no external source describes his party allegiance. None-found.

label: The Sadducees say there is no resurrection
statement: The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection.
note: The same doctrine Matthew 22:23 reports of the group (related_to). Josephus, Ant. 18.1.4: 'the doctrine of the Sadducees is this: That souls die with the bodies'; War 2.8.14: they 'take away the belief of the immortal duration of the soul' (grade A for the doctrine, as in Matthew 22).

label: The Sadducees say there is no angel nor spirit
statement: The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit.
note: Disputed: the fetched Wikipedia 'Sadducees' article states the Sadducees 'may have rejected the notion of spirits or angels' and that 'this is based on Acts 23:8, which can be translated' in two ways - older translations' 'no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit' is 'obviously not what the Greek means' per the article. Josephus (Ant. 18; War 2) records the Sadducees' denial of fate/providence and of the soul's survival but never mentions angels. None-found externally for the doctrine itself.

label: The Pharisees confess the resurrection
statement: The Pharisees confess the resurrection of the dead (with the angel and the spirit).
note: Josephus, Ant. 18.1.3: the Pharisees 'believe that souls have an immortal rigor in them', that there are rewards and punishments 'under the earth', and 'the former shall have power to revive and live again' - the same doctrine of a rising after death (grade A for the resurrection doctrine).

label: The Pharisees confess both angel and spirit
statement: The Pharisees confess both the angel and the spirit (as Acts 23:8-9 presupposes).
note: None-found: Josephus (Ant. 18.1.3; War 2.8.2-14) records the Pharisees' fate/providence and soul doctrines but never their angel-doctrine; the external Wikipedia 'Sadducees' article says the angels half of the contrast rests on Acts 23:8 itself and that the translation is disputed.

label: Scribes of the Pharisees' party contended, 'We find no evil in this man'
statement: A great clamor arose; some scribes of the Pharisees' part stood up and contended: 'We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let's not fight against God!'
note: The intervention is the narrative's own report; none-found.

label: The tribune, fearing Paul would be torn apart, sent soldiers to take him by force into the barracks
statement: When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing Paul would be torn in pieces, commanded the soldiers to go down, take him by force from among them and bring him into the barracks.
note: The barracks of the Antonia fortress are again the setting; the rescue itself has no external witness.

label: The Lord stood by Paul at night: 'You must testify also at Rome'
statement: The following night the Lord stood by Paul and said, 'Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.'
note: Vision claim; none-found in every external category.

label: More than forty Jews bound themselves by curse to kill Paul and asked the chief priests to have him brought down
statement: More than forty Jews bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor to drink until they had killed Paul; they asked the chief priests and elders to inform the tribune so that Paul would be brought down to the council, intending to kill him on the way.
note: The plot is the narrative's own report; Josephus records no such conspiracy. None-found.

label: The conspirators bound themselves under a curse of abstention from food and drink
statement: The conspirators 'bound themselves under a curse' (anathematized themselves) saying they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
note: Mishnah Nedarim 1:1 (redacted c. 200 CE, later than the events): a vow renders an object forbidden 'as though it were a sacrificial offering', and 'That which I eat of yours' already binds - the same institution of self-cursing vows of abstention (grade C; may not describe the practice of the 50s CE exactly).

label: Paul's sister's son learned of the ambush and told Paul, who had him taken to the tribune
statement: Paul's sister's son heard they were lying in wait, came into the barracks and told Paul; Paul had a centurion bring him to the tribune, who took him aside, heard the report, and sent him away charging him to tell no one.
note: Paul's unnamed nephew is known only from this narrative; none-found.

label: Two centurions were ordered to ready 200 soldiers, 70 horsemen and 200 spearmen to leave at the third hour of the night
statement: The tribune called two centurions: 'Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night', with animals for Paul.
note: 470 men in all. The size is the narrative's own figure; modern reference (source, not evidence node): auxiliary cohortes ran about 480 men (six centuriae of 80) and alae turmae of 30-32, so a mixed detachment of 200 foot, 70 horse and 200 spearmen is within the Roman unit structure (fetched Wikipedia 'Auxilia', grade C).

label: The tribune wrote Felix a letter: he had rescued a Roman, found no charge worthy of death or imprisonment, and sent him with his accusers
statement: The tribune's letter (23:26-30) states that he rescued Paul when he learned he was Roman, found him accused only of questions of their law, nothing worthy of death or imprisonment, and sent him to Felix, charging his accusers to appear before him.
note: The letter's self-serving framing ('when I came with the soldiers and rescued him', passing over the scourging order of 22:24-29) is the narrative's own document; no external witness. None-found.

label: The tribune bore the name Claudius Lysias and addressed 'the most excellent governor Felix'
statement: The letter opens: 'Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings' - naming the tribune of chapters 21-23 for the only time.
note: Grade C (naming custom): under Claudius new citizens took the emperor's nomen - Dio 60.17.7 records informers charging new citizens with 'not adopting Claudius' name' (fetched LacusCurtius page); the tribune's nomen Claudius fits enfranchisement under Claudius, and his 'bought it for a great price' (22:28) fits the same emperor's sale of the franchise. The honorific kratistos ('most excellent') has no separately fetched witness.

label: The soldiers took Paul by night to Antipatris; next day the horsemen went on and the foot returned
statement: The soldiers took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris; the next day, leaving the horsemen to go with him, they returned to the barracks.
note: Antipatris, built by Herod the Great on the Roman road between Caesarea and Jerusalem (fetched Wikipedia, place A), lies about 46 km from Jerusalem; the two legs (~46 km and ~44 km) are computed from coordinates (observation). The march itself has no external witness.

label: At Caesarea the letter was delivered to Felix, who asked what province Paul was from
statement: They came to Caesarea, delivered the letter to the governor and presented Paul; when Felix read it and learned Paul was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.'
note: Caesarea was the governors' official residence (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima'); the hearing promise is the narrative's own report.

label: Felix ordered Paul kept in Herod's palace (the praetorium) at Caesarea
statement: Felix commanded that Paul be kept in Herod's palace (te par autou paratheoresamenos 'in the praetorium of Herod') until his accusers arrived.
note: Herod's palace at Caesarea stood on the promontory jutting into the sea, with a decorative pool surrounded by stoas (fetched Wikipedia 'Caesarea Maritima'); the excavated promontory palace confirms the Herodian governor's residence in which the procurator housed prisoners (grade B for the building and setting, not for the event of Paul's lodging).

label: Josephus, Ant. 20.103 (Herod of Chalcis appoints Ananias son of Nedebaeus high priest)
author: Josephus
note: In Cumanus's procuratorship Herod king of Chalcis 'removed Joseph, the son of Camydus, from the high priesthood, and made Ananias, the son of Nebedeu, his successor' - c. 47/48 CE.

label: Josephus, Ant. 20.205-206 (Ananias's greed and his servants' violence over tithes)
author: Josephus
note: Under Albinus (62-63 CE) the high priest Ananias 'increased in glory every day' and 'was a great hoarder up of money'; his wicked servants took the priests' tithes by violence and beat those who resisted, so that some priests died of want.

label: Josephus, Ant. 20.137-144 (Felix made procurator of Judea; he takes Drusilla)
author: Josephus
note: 'SO Claudius sent Felix, the brother of Pallas, to take care of the affairs of Judea' (20.137); as procurator he saw and married Drusilla, Agrippa II's sister (20.141-144).

label: Tacitus, Histories 5.9 (Felix 'exercised the power of a king in the spirit of a slave')
author: Tacitus
note: 'Claudius entrusted the province of Judaea to the Roman Knights or to his own freedmen, one of whom, Antonius Felix, indulging in every kind of barbarity and lust, exercised the power of a king in the spirit of a slave.'

label: Tacitus, Annals 12.54 (Felix, governor of Judaea, 'could do any evil act with impunity')
author: Tacitus
note: 'Not equally moderate was his brother, surnamed Felix, who had for some time been governor of Judaea, and thought that he could do any evil act with impunity' - with Ventidius Cumanus holding Galilee while Felix held Samaria.

label: Mishnah Nedarim 1:1 (vows render things forbidden like an offering)
author: Judah the Prince (compiler)
note: A vow renders an object forbidden to oneself or others as though it were a sacrificial offering; 'That which I eat of yours' or 'that which I taste of yours' already binds. Later redaction; may not describe the practice of the 50s CE exactly.

label: Exodus 22:28 ('You shall not curse God, nor curse a ruler of your people')
author: traditionally Moses

author: Cassius Dio
note: Under Claudius many 'bought it from Messalina and the imperial freedmen'; the franchise was 'at first sold only for large sums' and was later so cheapened 'that a man could become a citizen by giving the right person some bits of broken glass' (60.17.5-6); informers accused new citizens of 'not adopting Claudius' name' (60.17.7).
